title: Free fall & g
examples: What is the value of g near the Earth's surface?
How can we calculate g using a simple experiment?
Does air resistance affect the calculated value of g?

explain.say: Today we learn about free fall motion. Free fall means falling only under gravity's pull. We ignore air resistance for these calculations. Gravity causes a constant downward acceleration.
The acceleration due to gravity is often written as g. Near Earth's surface, g is approximately nine point eight meters per second squared. This value is constant for objects falling near us.
When we measure g, we often use a simple experiment. We might drop an object and measure its time falling a known distance. This helps us find the value of g.
If we know the distance and time, we can use the equations of motion. Remember that the initial velocity is zero for a dropped object. This lets us solve for g.

faq.q: What is the value of g at sea level?
faq.a: The standard accepted value for g near Earth's surface is nine point eight meters per second squared. This is a very useful constant in physics problems.
asks: What is the value of acceleration due to gravity?
How much is g on Earth?

faq.q: Do I need to worry about air resistance in these problems?
faq.a: For introductory calculations, we are taught to ignore air resistance. This simplifies the problem greatly, assuming the object falls through a vacuum.
asks: When can I ignore air resistance?

faq.q: What equipment do I need to measure g?
faq.a: You usually need a meter rule or measuring tape for distance. You also need a stopwatch to accurately measure the time it takes to fall.
asks: What do I need to measure g?
What tools are used for this experiment?

faq.q: Does the height I drop the object affect g?
faq.a: For small heights, the value of g remains essentially constant. The change over large distances is very small for this level.
asks: Does the height matter for g?

faq.q: What is the formula relating distance, time, and g?
faq.a: The relevant equation is distance equals half times g times time squared. This comes from the equations of motion when initial velocity is zero.
asks: What equation do I use for free fall?
How do I find distance using time and g?

facts: The acceleration due to gravity, g, is approximately nine point eight meters per second squared.
In free fall, the only force acting on the object is gravity.
We assume air resistance is negligible when calculating the value of g.
The acceleration is constant throughout the fall.

quiz.say: If an object falls for two seconds, what is its acceleration?
quiz.why: The acceleration due to gravity, g, is the constant acceleration for free fall, which is nine point eight meters per second squared.

wrong.1: This suggests no acceleration is happening, which is incorrect because gravity is pulling the object down.
wrong.2: This incorrectly uses the time value in the calculation instead of the known value of g.
wrong.3: This incorrectly calculates g times time, forgetting that the formula uses time squared.

quiz.say: A ball dropped from a tower falls a distance of nineteen point six meters. What was the time it took?
quiz.why: We use the formula distance equals half times g times time squared. Solving for time gives two seconds.

wrong.0: This might result from incorrectly using the formula distance equals g times time.
wrong.1: This is too small a value and does not account for the full distance fallen.
wrong.2: This incorrectly assumes the time is equal to the distance.

quiz.say: If we measure g using a falling object, what must the initial velocity be?
quiz.why: When an object is simply dropped, it starts from rest, meaning its initial velocity is zero.

wrong.0: The initial velocity must be known at the start of the measurement, not the end.
wrong.1: The initial velocity must be zero because the object is dropped, not thrown.
wrong.3: This confuses the initial velocity with the acceleration due to gravity.
